rows: Employers must assess and manage significant risks from work-related violence and aggression.
Work-related violence includes verbal or online abuse as well as physical assault.
Workers and their representatives should be consulted when identifying hazards and controls.
Incident records, worker reports and task observation can help identify patterns and higher-risk situations.
Controls may include staffing, workplace design, communication, queuing, security and safe systems of work.
Training should match the foreseeable situations identified by the risk assessment.
Incidents should be reported, investigated and used to improve controls.
Affected workers should receive appropriate practical and psychological support.
A customer-facing occupation or neighbourhood statistic does not prove the risk faced by a particular worker.
Current risk depends on task, time, staffing, client behaviour, environment, controls and incident history.
Employers must consider risks to women of childbearing age in the general workplace risk assessment.
After written notification of pregnancy, recent birth or breastfeeding, an individual risk assessment is required.
The assessment should be reviewed as pregnancy, work or medical advice changes.
Identified risks should be avoided, removed or controlled so far as required by law.
Suitable alternative work may need to be offered before suspension on maternity grounds.
Pregnant and breastfeeding workers must have access to suitable rest facilities.
Night work may require adjustment where a doctor or midwife advises that it affects health.
Common considerations include physical load, chemicals, biological agents, radiation, fatigue and extreme temperature.
Pregnancy or breastfeeding does not make every work activity unsafe; assessment must be individual and evidence based.
A workplace classification cannot establish medical restrictions, exposure, fatigue or the suitability of adjustments.
Employers owe young people the same core health, safety and welfare duties as other workers.
Young workers may be at greater risk because of inexperience, immaturity and unfamiliarity with work.
Existing risk assessments should be reviewed before employing a young person for the first time or with particular needs.
Additional factors can include physical or psychological capacity, exposure to agents and lack of experience.
Training should be clear, understandable and proportionate to the task and the young person's experience.
Supervision should be closer while competence and safe behaviour are being established.
Young workers should know how to raise concerns and what work they are not authorised to perform.
Work-experience employers retain primary responsibility for workplace health and safety.
Age alone does not determine competence, but additional risk factors must be considered for people under 18.
A placement description cannot prove the quality of induction, supervision, task restrictions or risk controls.
Employers are responsible for the health, safety and welfare of disabled and non-disabled workers.
Health and safety law should not be used as an excuse to discriminate against disabled people.
Employers should review risk assessments where a disability could affect workplace safety.
Risk assessment should focus on the work and barriers rather than making assumptions about a diagnosis.
Equality law can require reasonable adjustments for disabled workers.
Adjustments may include physical changes, adapted equipment, altered duties, support or flexible arrangements.
Workers should be consulted about barriers and practical solutions.
Specialist advice may be needed where the effects of a condition on work are not clear.
A disability label does not establish that a person cannot safely perform a task.
Suitability depends on individual capability, barriers, adjustments, task demands and current consultation.
